title: The Ming Empire in China (1368–1644)
meta: Ebrey and Walthall · Chapter 14 · Opening questions, p. 227
description: The seven opening questions on page 227 of Ebrey and Walthall’s Ming chapter, with answers and evidence from pages 227–246.
overview: In 1376 the founding emperor of the Ming asked for criticism. Ye Boju wrote back that officials were being punished too severely for small mistakes. The emperor had Ye brought to the capital in chains. He died of starvation in prison. A century and a half later, officials were still willing to kneel outside the palace and challenge an emperor in public. p. 231 Go to question 6

sections.title: 1. How did China compare to Western Europe in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries?

body.p: Early in the fifteenth century, the Ming court could send a much larger expedition to sea than Columbus or Vasco da Gama would command later in the century. Zheng He’s first fleet left in 1405 with 317 ships. It followed routes merchants already used. The court wanted foreign rulers to send envoys, and Zheng He offered their representatives passage to China. Among the things his fleets brought home were African giraffes and Indian cotton. pp. 232–233

By the sixteenth century, Chinese and European merchants were buying from one another. Portuguese traders established a base at Macao in 1557. Silver from Mexico and Peru crossed the Pacific through Manila to pay for Chinese silk and porcelain. p. 234

sections.title: 2. Had China already begun to fall behind Western Europe in technology, standard of living, or pace of change?

body.p: Ebrey and Walthall give us a comparison of ships. They leave the comparison of living standards open. After the last voyage, Zheng He’s fleet sat in harbor. Officials had objected to the expense, the emperor who backed the voyages had died, and his successors faced a renewed Mongol threat. In 1474 the remaining ships with three or more masts were taken apart for lumber. pp. 232–233

For a household, the evidence would have to tell us what people could earn and what it cost to live. The authors describe tenant farmers, absentee landowners and wealthy lower Yangzi cities. By 1600 China had more towns, larger cities and more books in circulation. The chapter offers no equivalent European evidence for comparing households or measuring which society was changing faster. pp. 227, 246

sections.title: 3. At the local level, were communities becoming more integrated into the realm as standardizing policies and economic linkages spread?

body.p: Yes. A rule made at court could determine which family in a village had to collect the grain and haul it away. The first Ming emperor grew up fearing tax collectors. To protect villagers, he made better-off local families assess, collect and deliver taxes without pay. The burden could ruin households. Later reforms converted most of those obligations into payments of money. p. 240

Trade connected households across even greater distances. In 1639 Japan barred traders from Macao from entering Nagasaki. Soon afterward, trade between Chinese merchants and the Spanish in the Philippines stopped. Less silver reached China. Ebrey and Walthall trace part of the unrest over rents in the lower Yangzi to the resulting fall in prices, which made rents harder to pay. p. 245

sections.title: 4. Or were they becoming more diverse as the economy developed in different directions in different places?

body.p: Yes. The same water routes that brought regions into closer contact also made it profitable for them to grow or make different things. Farmers in coastal Fujian raised sugar cane and tobacco. Producers in the lower Yangzi delta concentrated on cotton and silk. At Jingdezhen, potters could sell porcelain far beyond the households that lived near their kilns. p. 240

Families organized differently, too. In Huizhou, merchants’ wealth helped sustain groups of relatives who traced descent from a common ancestor. Ebrey calls these groups lineages. Some owned land together and paid for a school or an ancestral temple. Lineages were more common in southern China than in the north. pp. 227, 240

sections.title: 5. How effective and how adaptable was the government?

body.p: The Ming founder restored order after the Yuan collapse. He also concentrated decisions so tightly at court that much depended on one man. In 1380 Zhu Yuanzhang eliminated the chancellor’s post and took reports directly from the heads of ministries. Two centuries later the Wanli emperor refused to hold court for years at a time. Officials’ reports piled up unopened and government posts stayed vacant. pp. 227, 229–230

On the coast, the government did change course. It first tried to deprive pirates of supplies by forcing residents to move inland. Ebrey and Walthall report that efforts against piracy began to work better when officials eased restrictions on maritime trade. p. 234

sections.title: 6. Why did educated men continue to seek office when the government so often treated them poorly?

body.p: A degree gave a family status. Office also gave a scholar a duty to speak when he thought the emperor was wrong. Even the lowest degree excused a man from compulsory labor. His relatives might pay for his schooling because the whole family gained standing if he passed. The highest degree qualified him for an appointment. Competition eventually surpassed the levels of the Song dynasty. pp. 227, 234–236

In 1519 more than a hundred officials knelt outside the palace to oppose Emperor Wuzong’s proposed tour of the southern provinces. He made them kneel for three days and then had them flogged. Eleven died. The Confucian tradition honored officials who took that risk. Others chose local posts where they could still do useful work, or retired if they could afford to. p. 231

sections.title: 7. What was the impact on the educated class of the changes in the examination system and the explosion of printing?

body.p: Exams trained candidates across China to read the same classics and write the same kind of essay. Print gave readers a much wider choice. Provincial quotas gave men outside the wealthy lower Yangzi a better chance to compete. Only about 2–4 percent of candidates passed the provincial exam. For many educated men, repeated attempts at that exam occupied much of their lives. pp. 234–236

Consider two kinds of reading. A candidate learned the Four Books with Zhu Xi’s interpretations. A reader of Journey to the West followed the Tang monk Xuanzang to India in the company of a supernatural monkey and a pig. Publishers competed for buyers of novels by adding pictures or commentary. Stories and plays written in everyday language also reached people with little classical schooling. pp. 227, 234, 242–244

readings: Patricia Buckley Ebrey and Anne Walthall, Pre-Modern East Asia: A Cultural, Social, and Political History, vol. I, 3rd ed., chapter 14, “The Ming Empire in China (1368–1644),” pp. 227–246. The seven questions are from printed p. 227; page numbers after each answer refer to the textbook.
